column1: Industrial electricity rate exemptions in the UK and Germany
Rules as described in section 4 of the article

column2: Make a product in one of 71 eligible manufacturing classes (steel, aluminium, cement, glass, paper, many chemicals — SI 2015/721 Schedule) and pass a firm-level intensity test: electricity costs of at least 20% of gross value added.
column3: Since 2023: be in a sector on a 116-class list (EnFG Anlage 2 — Germany’s energy-levies act, carrying the EU’s climate state-aid (CEEAG) list) and use ≥1 GWh a year — no firm-level intensity test on the list route. Until 2022 (EEG levy cap): an intensity test applied — electricity costs above 15% of gross value added and more than 10 GWh a year for benefit years 2010–12; at least 14% and 1 GWh in 2013; from 2014 a sector list plus 14–17% (list 1) or 20% (list 2). The network relief is gated separately, on operation alone.

column2: No. A two-shift site qualifies as easily as a baseload one.
column3: Decisively. The network floor needs more than 10 GWh a year and ≥7,000 full-load hours; a two-shift 20 GWh site at 5,000 hours qualifies for none of it.

column2: 100% exemption from RO, CfD and FiT — 85% from 2018, 100% from April 2024.
column3: The EEG-Umlage cap (BesAR) until mid-2022, when the levy moved to the federal budget for everyone.

column2: The certificate does not touch the Climate Change Levy — but a separate mineralogical and metallurgical exemption removes it automatically for the heaviest processes (steel, aluminium, cement, glass, lime, ceramics). Firms outside those processes hold a Climate Change Agreement instead, which discounts the levy by 92% rather than removing it — so the zero-levy relieved stacks below are a floor for e.g. a paper mill.
column3: Producing industry pays a reduced Stromsteuer (§9b), cut to near-zero from 2024.
